objectives: Describe the request and response cycle between a client and a server
Read common HTTP status codes such as 200 and 404
Explain why a server cannot trust the client

exercises.prompt: Draw the steps when you open a shopping app and tap 'My orders'. Label the client, the server, the request and the response.
exercises.answer: The app (client) sends a request such as GET /orders with proof of who you are. The server checks it, reads your orders from its database and sends a response with status 200 and the list. The app then draws the screen.

exercises.prompt: An app hides the 'Delete user' button from normal users. Is that enough to stop them deleting users? Why or why not?
exercises.answer: No. Hiding a button only changes the client, and a user can send the request by hand or modify the app. The server must check on every request that the caller is allowed to delete users.

practical.title: Watch a request happen
practical.task: Open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab and load any web page. Pick one request and note its method, URL, status code and how long it took. Then try curl -i on the same URL.
practical.done: You can point at one request and name its client, server, method, status code and response time.

objectives: Distinguish latency from throughput
Explain why percentiles such as p99 matter more than averages
Compare rough costs of memory, disk and network access

exercises.prompt: A coffee shop has 2 baristas and each coffee takes 3 minutes. What are the latency and the maximum throughput? What happens if 50 customers arrive in an hour?
exercises.answer: Latency is 3 minutes per coffee. Throughput is 2 baristas times 20 coffees per hour, so 40 per hour. With 50 arrivals the queue grows, so later customers wait much longer than 3 minutes even though each coffee still takes 3.

exercises.prompt: 1 million requests arrive per day. About how many per second is that on average, and how should you plan for peaks?
exercises.answer: A day has about 86,400 seconds, so 1 million per day is roughly 12 requests per second on average. Traffic is uneven, so plan for several times that at peak, around 5 to 10 times, and check the p99 latency at that load.

practical.title: Measure p50 and p99
practical.task: Write a small program that calls any HTTP URL 100 times in a row and records each time in milliseconds. Sort the results and read off the median (p50), the 99th value (p99) and the mean.
practical.done: You have the three numbers and can explain why the p99 and the mean differ.

objectives: Explain how a load balancer shares requests among servers
Describe how health checks remove failed servers
Explain why servers should be stateless behind a balancer

exercises.prompt: Three servers sit behind a round-robin balancer and server 2 crashes. Describe what should happen to requests 7 to 10.
exercises.answer: Health checks to server 2 fail, so the balancer removes it. Requests then alternate between servers 1 and 3, so users still get answers. When server 2 passes health checks again it is added back.

exercises.prompt: Your login is stored in the memory of one app server, and users are randomly logged out. Why, and how do you fix it?
exercises.answer: The balancer sends some requests to other servers that do not hold the session. Fix it by storing sessions in a shared store such as Redis or using signed tokens, so any server can serve any user. Sticky routing is a weaker fix because it ties users to one server.

practical.title: Balance two servers
practical.task: Run two copies of a tiny web app that each print their own name, and put Nginx or another proxy in front of them with round-robin. Request it 10 times, then stop one copy and request again.
practical.done: You saw the answers alternate between both servers, and after stopping one you can say how the balancer stopped sending it traffic.

objectives: Estimate load and capacity with back-of-envelope numbers
Explain consistent hashing and why it helps
Scale on the signal that's actually the bottleneck

exercises.prompt: You add a fourth cache node to three, using hash(key) mod N. Roughly what fraction of keys move? What about with consistent hashing?
exercises.answer: With mod N, about three quarters of keys remap, which causes a stampede on the database. With consistent hashing only about a quarter move, the share taken over by the new node, and virtual nodes keep that share even.

exercises.prompt: Your service's pods autoscale on CPU, but latency climbs while CPU stays low. Why might that happen, and what signal would you scale on?
exercises.answer: The work is mostly waiting on I/O, or it's limited by a connection pool or queue, so CPU never reflects the load. Scale on what actually saturates: in-flight requests, queue depth or latency. Also check whether the true bottleneck is downstream, because adding pods won't help then, and can make things worse.

practical.title: Find a real limit
practical.task: Load test any small HTTP service with k6, hey or similar, raising concurrency until latency bends upward. Identify what saturated first: CPU, connections, a database or a thread pool.
practical.done: You have the load at which it degraded and evidence of what limited it, not just a requests-per-second number.

objectives: Choose a cache pattern and an invalidation approach
Prevent a cache stampede
Explain the race in cache-aside writes

exercises.prompt: In cache-aside, why is it safer to delete the cache entry on write rather than update it? What race can still happen?
exercises.answer: If two writers update the cache, they can apply in the opposite order to the database, leaving a stale value indefinitely. Deleting avoids that. A race remains: a reader misses and reads the old value, a writer updates and deletes, and then the reader stores the stale value. TTLs limit how long this lasts, and delayed double-delete or leases reduce it.

exercises.prompt: A popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Name three ways to prevent this.
exercises.answer: Request coalescing or a lock, so that only one caller recomputes the value. Serving stale while one caller refreshes it, or refreshing early before it expires. Adding random jitter to TTLs so that many keys don't expire together.

practical.title: Create and fix a stampede
practical.task: Put a small cache in front of a deliberately slow function. Send 100 concurrent requests just after expiry and count the backend calls. Add request coalescing and count again.
practical.done: You've measured backend calls before and after, for example 100 versus 1.

objectives: Design resource-based endpoints using nouns and HTTP methods
Choose suitable status codes for success and errors
Make create operations safe to retry and lists safe to page through

exercises.prompt: Design the endpoints for a to-do app: add a task, list tasks, mark one done, delete one. Give method, path and a success status for each.
exercises.answer: POST /tasks returns 201; GET /tasks?page=1 returns 200; PUT or PATCH /tasks/{id} returns 200 to mark done; DELETE /tasks/{id} returns 204 or 200. Paths are nouns and methods are the verbs.

exercises.prompt: A mobile client times out on 'POST /payments' and retries. How do you stop the customer being charged twice?
exercises.answer: Have the client send an idempotency key unique to that payment attempt. The server stores the key with the result and, on a repeat, returns the stored result instead of charging again.

practical.title: Build a tiny orders API
practical.task: Using ASP.NET Core minimal APIs or any framework, build POST /orders, GET /orders/{id} and GET /orders?page=1 with an in-memory list. Return 201, 200 and 404 correctly, then call it with curl.
practical.done: All three endpoints answer with the right status codes, and a missing id returns 404 rather than 200.

objectives: Choose a queue or pub/sub from the requirement
Design consumers for at-least-once delivery
Handle ordering, retries and poison messages

exercises.prompt: Your broker delivers at least once. A payment consumer crashes after charging but before acknowledging. What happens, and how do you make it safe?
exercises.answer: The message is redelivered and the customer could be charged twice. Make the consumer idempotent: record the message or payment key in the same transaction as the side effect and skip keys you've seen, or pass an idempotency key to the payment provider.

exercises.prompt: How does Kafka order messages, and what breaks that order for a single entity?
exercises.answer: Order is guaranteed only within a partition, so keying by entity ID keeps one entity's messages in order. It breaks if the key changes, the partition count changes (the key then maps elsewhere), messages are retried out of order by a producer without idempotence, or a consumer processes one partition concurrently.

practical.title: Build an idempotent consumer
practical.task: Run RabbitMQ or Kafka locally. Write a consumer that crashes at random after doing its work but before acknowledging. Observe the duplicates, then add an idempotency check.
practical.done: Across repeated crashes every message took effect exactly once, even though it was delivered more than once.

objectives: Explain CAP and PACELC accurately
Solve the dual-write problem with an outbox
Choose between a saga and a distributed transaction

exercises.prompt: A service updates its database and then publishes an event. What can go wrong, and how does the outbox pattern fix it?
exercises.answer: A crash between the two steps leaves the database updated with no event, or the reverse if the order is swapped. There's no atomic commit across both systems. With an outbox, you write the event to a table in the same database transaction, and a separate relay publishes it. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

exercises.prompt: Someone says "we chose AP, so we don't have consistency". What's wrong with that statement?
exercises.answer: CAP only describes behaviour during a network partition, and only for linearizability. Outside a partition, the real trade-off is latency against consistency, which is what PACELC adds. Most systems also offer many models between strong and eventual, such as read-your-writes or causal, and the choice can be made per operation.

practical.title: Implement an outbox
practical.task: In a small service with a database, write an order and its event in one transaction, and publish from a relay process. Kill the relay partway through and restart it.
practical.done: No event was lost, you've seen at least one duplicate or handled the case, and you can say why consumers must be idempotent.
